einzeiler: Why Americans are having fewer children than they want and what might help fix it.
kurzfassung: The U.S. and other nations face a growing fertility gap where people are having fewer children than they desire. While cash handouts show limited results, new research points to remote work and affordable housing as key drivers. Addressing these practical hurdles could help close the gap and fulfill family aspirations.
stichpunkte: Global fertility rates have fallen by more than half since 1970, with the U.S. seeing a steady decline since the 2007 recession.
Surveys show most Americans want between two and 2.7 children, meaning the true crisis is a fertility gap rather than low preferences.
Traditional cash incentives and tax credits have a negligible or zero impact on boosting long-term birth rates.
Intensive parenting norms and high-end expectations, such as travel sports, make raising children feel like a costly 18-year logistical hassle.
Smartphones and social incapacitation have contributed to a significant drop in face-to-face socialization and delayed marriage.
Remote work correlates with roughly 300,000 extra U.S. births a year, providing couples the necessary flexibility.
Historical analysis of the baby boom reveals that government-backed mortgages and early homeownership drove substantial increases in fertility.

clips.text: Half of all women reach age 30 without having started a family, and overcoming this deficit later in life presents nearly impossible biological odds.

clips.hook: A nine-dollar pint of blueberries from Peru
clips.text: Modern parenting has transformed into an expensive, boutique experience compared to the cheap and simple provisions of past generations.

clips.hook: Remote work adds nearly half a child extra per couple
clips.text: Couples who regularly work from home experience a substantial increase in family size compared to those in the office five days a week.

beschreibung:
Americans are having fewer children than they want. Government attempts to boost birth rates haven’t done much. But new research points to a surprisingly simple way to help — and it starts at home. (Part one of a two-part series.)

SOURCES:Nick Bloom, professor of economics at Stanford University.
Melissa Kearney, professor of economics at the University of Notre Dame.
Lyman Stone, director of the Pronatalism Initiative at the Institute for Family Studies.

RESOURCES:"Does Remote Work Increase Fertility?" by Andrew C. Johnston (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).
"Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly," by Caitlin K. Meyers and Ezekiel Hooper (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).
"Work from Home and Fertility," by Steven J. Davis, Cevat Giray Aksoy, Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, Katelyn Cranney, Mathias Dolls, and Pablo Zarate (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).
"Why is Fertility so Low in High Income Countries?" by Melissa Schettini Kearney and Phillip B. Levine (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2025).
"Can Housing Policy Raise Birth Rates? Lessons from Federal Mortgage Programs During the Baby Boom," by Lisa J. Dettling and Melissa Schettini Kearney (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2025).
